nameStory: The pectoral sandpiper gets its name from the distinctive streaked breast patch that resembles a pectoral muscle or chest area. This 'pectoral' marking is one of the bird's most reliable identifying features, standing out like a bib against its lighter belly.
description: The pectoral sandpiper is a medium-sized shorebird that's slightly larger than many of its sandpiper cousins, measuring about 8-9 inches long with wings that span up to 18 inches. It has a compact, sturdy build with brownish streaked upperparts and a distinctive streaked breast that cuts off sharply at a white belly. This arctic breeder is a long-distance traveler, passing through New England during spring and fall migrations on its way between northern breeding grounds and South American wintering areas.

idTips.label: Streaked breast pattern
idTips.description: Look for heavy dark streaking across the breast that stops abruptly at a clean white belly line, creating a sharp contrast like someone drew a line across the bird's chest

idTips.label: Size and posture
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than least sandpipers, with a more upright stance when feeding - appears chunky and substantial compared to smaller 'peeps'

idTips.label: Bill shape
idTips.description: Straight, dark bill that's longer than the head but not dramatically long - feels proportional to the bird's stocky build

idTips.label: Leg color
idTips.description: Yellowish to greenish legs that can appear muddy or dull, never bright orange-yellow like some other sandpipers

idTips.label: Feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often feeds with head down in a methodical, almost mechanical picking motion, staying in one area longer than more nervous sandpipers

habitat: Look for pectoral sandpipers in mudflats, shallow pond edges, flooded fields, and grassy marsh borders throughout New England during migration. They prefer areas with soft, muddy substrates where they can probe for invertebrates, and are often found in inland locations as well as coastal areas. Agricultural fields with standing water or recently harvested cranberry bogs are particularly attractive to these birds.

seasonality.spring: Present during migration from late April through May, often in small flocks mixed with other sandpipers. Look for birds in breeding plumage with more contrasted streaking.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in New England during summer months as most birds continue north to Arctic breeding grounds. Occasional non-breeding individuals may linger.
seasonality.fall: Peak migration occurs from July through September, with juveniles showing up later in the season. Fall birds may appear slightly less streaky than spring migrants.
seasonality.winter: Not present in New England during winter months - these birds continue south to South America for the cold season.

funFact: Male pectoral sandpipers have inflatable throat sacs that they use during courtship displays on their Arctic breeding grounds, puffing up like tiny feathered balloons while making hooting sounds that can be heard over half a mile away!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with least sandpipers, but pectorals are noticeably larger with that sharp breast-to-belly contrast. Remember: 'Pectoral = Pecs' - think of that defined chest muscle line that stops abruptly, while least sandpipers have streaking that fades gradually into the belly.
compareHints: Among the Calidris sandpipers in New England, pectoral sandpipers are distinguished by their larger size and that signature sharp breast line - dunlin have curved bills and different streaking, while the various 'peeps' (least, semipalmated) are much smaller. White-rumped sandpipers are similar in size but show white rumps in flight and have different breast patterns with streaking extending down the flanks.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the Calidris sandpipers, sanderlings are notably stockier with a thicker bill than the needle-billed Least Sandpiper or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Within the Calidris genus, Semipalmated Sandpipers are most similar to Western Sandpipers but have blunter, shorter bills and less rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among its Calidris cousins, the Least Sandpiper's yellow-green legs immediately set it apart from the black-legged Semipalmated and Sanderling.

Among the Calidris sandpipers, dunlin are larger than the "peeps" (semipalmated, least, and white-rumped sandpipers) but smaller than red knot, with that diagnostic curved bill that none of the others possess.
Among the many Calidris sandpipers, Purple Sandpiper is unique for its consistently dark plumage and exclusive rocky habitat preference.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, White-rumped is most similar to Baird's Sandpiper, but Baird's lacks the white rump and has a more buff-colored breast.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Red Knot is the second-largest and most robust, much chunkier than Sanderling or Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, the Stilt Sandpiper is the tallest and longest-legged, easily distinguished from the tiny 'peeps' like Least and Semipalmated Sandpipers.
Among the small Calidris sandpipers, Baird's stands out with its notably long wing projection past the tail - much longer than Semipalmated or Least Sandpipers.
Among New England's Calidris sandpipers, Buff-breasted is unique for its solid peachy-tan underparts and preference for grassy areas over mudflats.

Among New England's small sandpipers, Western Sandpipers are most easily confused with Semipalmated Sandpipers, but Westerns have longer, more drooped bill tips and often show more rusty coloring in breeding plumage.
Among Calidris sandpipers, Ruffs are unique in their extreme sexual size difference - much more pronounced than in Dunlin or Pectoral Sandpipers.
Among its Calidris sandpiper relatives, the Curlew Sandpiper's curved bill immediately sets it apart from straight-billed species like Sanderling and Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Among its Calidris relatives in New England, Little Stint is smaller than Least Sandpiper (already our tiniest regular sandpiper) and much smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper.
Compared to other small Calidris sandpipers in New England, Red-necked Stint is smaller than Semipalmated Sandpiper and has darker legs than Least Sandpiper.
Among the Calidris sandpipers, Sharp-tailed is most similar to Pectoral Sandpiper in size and habitat preferences, but lacks the Pectoral's sharply cut breast band.
Among Calidris sandpipers, the Surfbird is uniquely stocky and rock-adapted, unlike its beach and mudflat-loving relatives.
